record.paper_title: The Interiors of Uranus and Neptune: Current Understanding and Open Questions
record.original_question: How are the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune generated: which electrically conducting materials and convective regions exist inside each planet, how much water or other material is required to create an ionic or super-ionic interior, and how can magnetic-field structure and variability constrain the planetary interiors?

evidence.quote: Key fundamental questions regarding Uranus and Neptune remain open, such as: Key questions regarding Uranus and Neptune include: +How is the magnetic field generated?

Better determining the structure and potential variability of the planetary magnetic fields will allow us to further constrain the planetary structure via the required conditions to sustain a dynamo (electrically conducting material + convection).

Although the argument that the planets must consist of large fractions of water to have high enough electrical conductivities (ionic/super-ionic water) to generate their magnetic fields is convincing, it is yet to be determined how much water is required and whether other materials could contribute to the ionic interior.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a model ice-giant planet consisting of concentric layers of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rock, in hydrostatic equilibrium under self-gravity, with an equation of state and conductivity profile σ(ρ,T,X) (depending on density ρ, temperature T, and composition X) appropriate to high-pressure mixtures of these constituents. Suppose the planet supports a magnetohydrodynamic dynamo governed by the standard Boussinesq (or anelastic) MHD equations

  ∂_t u + (u·∇)u = −(1/ρ)∇p + ν∇²u − 2Ω×u + (1/μ_0 ρ)(∇×B)×B + buoyancy,
  ∂_t B = ∇×(u×B) + (1/μ_0 σ)∇²B,
  ∇·B = 0,

in a rotating spherical shell, with convection driven by an internal heat flux. The observed surface magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are strongly non-axisymmetric and non-dipolar, with substantial quadrupole and octupole contributions.

Determine, within this framework:

(a) Which interior regions (specified by radial extent and composition) must be simultaneously electrically conducting and convecting in order to sustain a dynamo producing surface magnetic fields with the observed multipole spectrum and morphology of Uranus and Neptune.

(b) The minimum mass fraction (and corresponding radial distribution) of H₂O required, given current high-pressure equations of state and ab initio conductivity data for ionic and super-ionic water, for the conducting layer to attain magnetic Reynolds numbers Rm = UL/(η) sufficient (Rm ≳ 50) to drive such a dynamo; and whether other candidate constituents (e.g. ionic ammonia, hydrogen–helium mixtures, or rocky/silicate phases at high P,T) can substitute for or supplement water in providing the required conductivity.

(c) What quantitative constraints on the interior density, composition, and convective structure can be inferred from improved measurements of the spatial structure and secular variability of the surface magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune.
artifact.status_search_result: The generation mechanism of the non-dipolar magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune, the precise composition and depth of the conducting convective layer, and the minimum required water content remain active open research problems. Thin-shell convective dynamo models (Stanley & Bloxham 2004, 2006) reproduce the observed multipolar morphology qualitatively, but the underlying interior composition is not uniquely determined; recent ab initio studies of super-ionic H₂O, NH₃, and H–C–N–O mixtures continue to refine but have not settled the question. New constraints await a dedicated Uranus or Neptune orbiter mission.

status_evidence.title: Stanley & Bloxham, Convective-region geometry as the cause of Uranus' and Neptune's unusual magnetic fields
status_evidence.snippet: Thin-shell dynamo models in a stably stratified fluid interior can reproduce the non-axisymmetric, non-dipolar fields of Uranus and Neptune, but the precise interior structure remains uncertain.
status_evidence.claim: Composition/geometry of the dynamo region is constrained but not uniquely determined.

status_evidence.title: Helled, Nettelmann & Guillot, Uranus and Neptune: Origin, Evolution and Internal Structure
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews state that the conducting layer is consistent with ionic/super-ionic water, but the required water mass fraction and contributions of other ices are not yet quantitatively determined.
status_evidence.claim: Required water content and alternative conducting constituents remain open.

status_evidence.title: Soderlund & Stanley, The underexplored frontier of ice giant dynamos
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies the dynamo mechanism, conducting-region depth, and link to interior composition as key open problems for Uranus and Neptune.
status_evidence.claim: The magnetic-field generation problem is explicitly listed as open.
